headline: OpenAI Shuts Down Russian Accounts That Misused ChatGPT to Spread Propaganda

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: OpenAI is the company that makes a computer program called ChatGPT, which can chat with people and write text. Some people in Russia broke the rules to use ChatGPT even though they were not supposed to. They used special tools called VPNs, which hide where someone is really located, to trick the system. These people used ChatGPT to write posts and comments and shared them on websites like Facebook, LinkedIn, and Telegram. They pretended to be part of a smart 'expert group' called the International Burke Institute. This group had a website with articles, but many of the articles were actually copied from other people's work. They also made a made-up scoring system that made Russia look very strong and good compared to other countries. OpenAI noticed something was strange, investigated, and found this whole hidden plan. They then banned the accounts. This matters because it shows people can misuse smart computer tools to spread messages that are not fully true, and companies need to watch out for this kind of trickery.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: OpenAI, the company behind the popular AI chatbot ChatGPT, discovered that a group of people in Russia had been secretly using its tool to run an influence operation — a hidden campaign meant to shape what people believe. To get around location blocks, they used VPNs, tools that disguise a user's real location online. With ChatGPT's help, they created posts and comments that were shared across platforms like Substack, Telegram, X, Facebook, and LinkedIn. Most of this content was written in English, and the group even asked ChatGPT to remove any hints that might reveal they were Russian. Their main project was promoting something called the International Burke Institute, which claimed to be a serious research group based in Israel. However, many of the 'expert' articles on its website were actually copied from real academic work, sometimes crediting the wrong authors. The group also invented a 'Sovereignty Index' that ranked countries and made Russia appear strong and successful while criticizing Western nations. Although the campaign didn't reach huge numbers of people — some Telegram channels had around 10,000 to 20,000 followers — OpenAI says what's concerning is how the operation used AI to help build a fake sense of authority and credibility. This story shows how new AI tools can be misused to spread misleading information, and why companies must stay alert to catch and stop this kind of activity.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: OpenAI recently uncovered and shut down a network of Russian-linked ChatGPT accounts that were part of a coordinated influence operation — a secret effort to sway public opinion using misleading or manipulated information. The individuals behind it used VPNs (services that hide a person's true internet location) to bypass restrictions and access ChatGPT from Russia. They then used the AI to help generate social media posts and comments spread across sites like Telegram, X, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Substack, mostly written in English, while deliberately trying to erase any language clues that might reveal their Russian origins. The heart of the operation was a fake 'think tank' called the International Burke Institute, which claimed to be a global team of experts on politics, economics, and international relations. Investigators found that much of the content on its website was plagiarized from real academic sources, sometimes with incorrect authors listed, while other pieces appeared to be written by a Russian speaker and then translated into English using machine translation. The group also created a 'Sovereignty Index,' a made-up scoring system that ranked countries based on things like military strength, economy, and technology. Conveniently, it ranked Russia very favorably while portraying Western countries less positively. While the campaign's direct audience was relatively small — some Telegram channels reached only 10,000–20,000 followers — OpenAI emphasized that the real danger wasn't the size of the audience but the infrastructure: a professional-looking institute, fake experts, and a seemingly credible data-driven index, all designed to make propaganda look like independent research. This case matters because it reveals how AI tools, even when used only for small tasks like writing posts, can support much larger schemes to manufacture false credibility and spread hidden agendas — and how those same AI interactions can eventually help investigators trace and expose the operation.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: OpenAI announced that it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts tied to Russian operators who were running a coordinated influence operation, a term used to describe organized efforts to secretly shape public opinion, often by disguising the true source of the information. To get around geographic restrictions, the operators used VPNs (Virtual Private Networks), tools that mask a user's real location so they appear to be browsing from somewhere else. Using ChatGPT, they generated promotional social media posts and comments that were spread across multiple platforms, including Telegram, X, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Substack. Nearly all of the content was written in English, and the operators specifically instructed ChatGPT to remove any wording patterns that might reveal a Russian source. The centerpiece of the campaign was the International Burke Institute (IBI), presented as an independent 'expert community' based in Israel that studied politics, economics, and international relations. However, investigators found that much of the material on IBI's website was copied from legitimate academic research, sometimes falsely attributed to different authors, while other content appeared to be originally written in a Slavic language and then run through machine translation into English. Perhaps most notably, IBI promoted a 'Sovereignty Index,' a self-created ranking system measuring countries across seven categories such as military, economic, and technological strength. The index conveniently placed Russia among the top nations while praising its 'record military and economic self-sufficiency' and downplaying its weaknesses. Although the operation reached a relatively modest audience — some Telegram channels attracted 10,000 to 20,000 followers — OpenAI stressed that its true significance lay not in audience size but in the infrastructure being built: a seemingly credible institute complete with fabricated experts, republished research, and a fake proprietary index, all designed to lend false authority to pro-Russian narratives. This case illustrates a broader concern in the age of generative AI: bad actors don't need AI to do everything — even limited use, like writing a handful of promotional posts, can support a much larger scheme meant to manufacture legitimacy and obscure its true origins. At the same time, OpenAI noted that this same reliance on AI tools left digital traces that ultimately helped expose the entire operation, showing that AI misuse can be a double-edged sword for those who attempt it.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: OpenAI disclosed that it had identified and banned a network of ChatGPT accounts operated from Russia that were engaged in what it classified as a coordinated influence operation — a covert campaign designed to shape public discourse while concealing the identity and motives of those behind it. To circumvent geographic access restrictions, the operators relied on VPNs (Virtual Private Networks), which reroute internet traffic to disguise a user's true location. Through ChatGPT, they generated social media posts and comments that were disseminated across Substack, Telegram, X, Facebook, and LinkedIn, predominantly in English, while explicitly instructing the AI to eliminate any linguistic markers that might expose their Russian origin. The campaign's central vehicle was the International Burke Institute (IBI), a self-styled think tank based in Israel that presented itself as a global community of experts in economics, politics, sociology, and international relations. OpenAI's investigation revealed that much of IBI's published content had been lifted from legitimate academic sources, in some cases with false authorship attributed, while other material appeared to have been originally composed in a Slavic language and subsequently machine-translated into English. Notably, there was no direct evidence that ChatGPT was used to write these core articles — its confirmed role was limited to generating promotional social media content. The operation's most distinctive feature was the creation of a 'Sovereignty Index' (also called the Burke Index), a proprietary-looking metric assessing nations across seven dimensions — political, economic, technological, informational, cultural, cognitive, and military sovereignty — using a scoring system that appeared methodologically rigorous. The index ranked Russia favorably, just behind the United States and China, and included glowing language about Russia's 'record military and economic self-sufficiency' and its status as one of only three nations with 'full digital and military nuclear sovereignty,' while subtly acknowledging challenges like demographic decline and limited economic flexibility. Despite the operation's ambition, its direct reach was modest — leading Telegram channels amassed only 10,000 to 20,000 followers, and one account even used ChatGPT to design a profile picture for a channel called 'American Observer,' along with periodic Russian-language summaries of that channel's engagement. OpenAI emphasized that the operation's real significance lies not in its limited audience but in the underlying infrastructure it constructed: a professional-seeming institution complete with fabricated experts, republished scholarship, and an ostensibly data-driven credibility metric — all designed to manufacture legitimacy for narratives favorable to Russian interests while obscuring their true source. This case underscores a broader pattern emerging in AI-related security research: influence operations increasingly use generative AI not to create entire disinformation ecosystems from scratch, but as a supporting tool within larger schemes to scale outputs, obscure authorship, and lend surface-level credibility to fabricated institutions. Paradoxically, this reliance on AI tools also generated identifiable behavioral patterns and digital footprints, which is precisely what allowed OpenAI's investigators to detect and dismantle the operation before it could grow further.

questions: If you saw a post online from an 'expert institute' you had never heard of, what steps could you take to check if the information was trustworthy?
Why do you think it matters that AI tools like ChatGPT can be used to make fake organizations seem more believable, and how might this affect what you see on social media?
How do you think companies, schools, and everyday people should work together to spot and stop misleading information created with AI?
